answer.rationale: The release 2h ago is the only new variable that precedes the 90-minute latency climb, so it is the leading suspect and rollback is the intervention that addresses cause rather than symptom. But the inherited record is thinner than it looks. memory_b1 is the memory actually carrying the decision, and it describes a checkout ERROR spike cleared by rollback, not a gradual write-path LATENCY climb, and says nothing about whether that rollback happened under peak write load. I want the archived source to check whether the failure signature and traffic conditions actually match today, or whether b1 has been generalized into 'rollback works' beyond what it supports. I also want memory_b5 verified because it is the one competing hypothesis that directly names write latency recovery: if the original record shows the primary was saturated by read contention rather than by a code change, then read-replica routing is the better single move and rollback would burn the only window on the wrong cause. I am deliberately not verifying b2, b3, b4 — failover, capacity, and circuit breakers all treat symptoms and none explain a climb that starts right after a deploy. Real risks I am holding open: the 30-minute gap between deploy and onset is consistent with a slow leak or lock-contention regression but also with load simply crossing a threshold at settlement peak, in which case the release is innocent and rollback buys nothing. And rollback during peak settlement writes is not free — a schema or migration-bearing release can drop or corrupt in-flight writes on reversal, which violates the 'without losing customer writes' constraint more severely than the latency itself. So I intend a guarded staged rollback on a limited cohort first, per the canary lesson in memory_b6, watching write-path p99 on that slice before going wider; if the archive shows b1's rollback was migration-free and signature-matched, I widen, and if b5 shows read contention on the primary, I switch directions rather than committing to the inherited default.
